js-basics:1.explanation: var is hoisted and initialised to undefined, so typeof x is 'undefined'. let is hoisted but stays in the temporal dead zone until its declaration, so reading y throws a ReferenceError.
const prevents rebinding the variable, not mutating the object it points to. Assigning to a const throws a TypeError, and o.n stays 2.
In sloppy mode, function declarations in blocks are hoisted to function scope, so f is visible outside. The inner let a is block-scoped and doesn't touch the outer one.

js-basics:2.code: console.log(typeof typeof 1, typeof [], typeof function(){}, typeof undefined);
js-basics:2.explanation: typeof always returns a string, so typeof typeof 1 is 'string'. Arrays are 'object', functions report 'function', and undefined reports 'undefined'.

js-basics:2.code: console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3, Number.isInteger(5.0), Object.is(NaN, NaN), NaN === NaN);
js-basics:2.explanation: Binary floating point can't represent 0.1 and 0.2 exactly. 5.0 is the integer 5. Object.is treats NaN as equal to itself, while === does not.
BigInt is a separate primitive. console.log prints BigInt values with an n suffix, and 2n ** 64n is larger than the safe integer limit.

js-basics:3.explanation: + concatenates if either side is a string, while - and * convert to numbers. [] + [] is '' (both become empty strings), and [] + {} is '[object Object]'.

js-basics:3.code: console.log(null == undefined, null === undefined, null == 0, null >= 0);
js-basics:3.explanation: null == undefined is true by spec and null == 0 is false because == doesn't convert null to a number. Relational operators do convert, so null >= 0 is true. A famous quirk.
With ==, an object is converted to a primitive and booleans to numbers. [] becomes '' then 0, [0] becomes '0' then 0, and [1,2] becomes '1,2'.
Unary + uses ToNumber: empty or whitespace strings become 0, a trailing unit makes it NaN, null is 0, undefined is NaN and an empty array becomes '' then 0.

js-basics:4.explanation: || falls through on any falsy value, while ?? only on null or undefined. NaN || null evaluates to the last operand, null. The empty string prints as nothing.

js-basics:4.code:
const u = { a: { b: null } };
console.log(u?.a?.b?.c, u.x?.y.z, u.a?.['b']);
js-basics:4.explanation: Optional chaining short-circuits the whole rest of the chain at the first nullish value, so u.x?.y.z is undefined without evaluating .z. u.a?.['b'] is null, which isn't skipped because it's the final value.

js-basics:4.explanation: Falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, '', null, undefined and NaN. The string '0', empty arrays and empty objects are truthy.

js-basics:5.code:
for (const k in [10, 20]) console.log(typeof k);
for (const v of 'hi') console.log(v);
js-basics:5.explanation: for...in iterates enumerable property keys, which are always strings even for arrays. for...of iterates values from the iterable, here the characters of the string.
for...in visits all enumerable keys including added properties and inherited ones, so extra shows up. for...of uses the iterator, which only yields the indexed elements.
switch jumps to the matching case and falls through to following cases until a break. case 3 adds 3, then case 4 adds 4, then break stops.

js-basics:6.code:

console.log(s.at(-1), s.slice(-3, -1), s.substring(3, 1), s.substr(1, 2));
js-basics:6.explanation: at(-1) counts from the end. slice supports negatives, substring swaps its arguments when start > end (so 3,1 is 1,3 giving 'el'), and substr takes a start and a length.
split's second argument limits the number of pieces. padStart adds filler at the front, trim drops the spaces and repeat concatenates.
Template literals evaluate any expression. String length counts UTF-16 code units, and an emoji outside the BMP takes two, while spreading iterates by code point.

js-basics:7.code:

console.log(a.sort(), [...a].sort((x, y) => y - x));
js-basics:7.explanation: The default sort compares elements as strings, so '100' < '20' < '3'. Passing a numeric comparator fixes the order. sort also mutates the original array.
splice mutates: it removes 2 items from index 1, inserts 'x' and returns the removed items. slice never mutates.

js-basics:7.code: console.log([1, 2, 3].reduce((acc, n) => acc + n), [].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 'init'), [[1], [2, [3]]].flat(), [1, 2, 3].map(parseInt));
js-basics:7.explanation: flat() defaults to depth 1. map passes (value, index) so parseInt(2, 1) is NaN (radix 1 invalid) and parseInt(3, 2) is NaN (3 isn't a binary digit). reduce on an empty array returns the initial value.
Shrinking length truncates. Assigning past the end creates holes, which aren't the same as undefined values: the in operator reports false for them.

js-basics:8.code:
const { a, b: { c = 5, ...rest }, ...others } = { a: 1, b: { d: 2 }, e: 3, f: 4 };
console.log(a, c, rest, others);
js-basics:8.explanation: Destructuring supports defaults, renaming and rest at each level. c takes its default because the property is missing, rest collects the remaining nested keys, others collects the remaining top-level keys.
Spread makes a shallow copy and later keys override earlier ones, so b.x is 9 and a.x stays 1. y is the same nested object in both, so changing b.y.z changes a.y.z.

js-basics:8.code:
const o = { b: 1, 2: 'x', a: 2, 1: 'y' };
console.log(Object.keys(o), Object.values(o));
js-basics:8.explanation: Property order is integer-like keys in ascending order first, then string keys in insertion order. Keys are always strings.

js-basics:9.explanation: floor goes toward -Infinity, trunc toward zero, and Math.round rounds halves toward +Infinity (so -1.5 becomes -1). 1.005 is actually stored slightly below 1.005, so toFixed(2) gives 1.00.
Past 2^53 integers can't all be represented, so both sums round to the same double. Remainder keeps the sign of the dividend, and ** is right associative: 3 ** 2 = 9, then 2 ** 9.

js-functions:1.explanation: Each call pushes a frame on the call stack and runs to completion before returning to the caller, so b finishes inside a.

js-functions:2.explanation: Inside f, var a is hoisted to the top of f's scope and is undefined when logged, so it shadows the outer a. The outer a is untouched.

js-functions:3.explanation: JavaScript uses lexical scope: a function looks up variables where it was defined, not where it is called. inner was created inside outer, so x is 'outer'.

js-functions:4.explanation: Each call to counter creates a fresh scope, and each returned pair of closures shares that scope's n.
The IIFE copies the current i into its own parameter j, so each closure keeps a different value. This is what let does automatically per iteration.

js-functions:6.explanation: bind creates a function with a permanent this and pre-filled arguments, so call can't override this. Only the remaining argument changes. apply spreads an array.
A bound function can't be re-bound: the first bind wins.

js-functions:7.explanation: The curried function gathers arguments until it has f.length of them, then calls f, however they are split across calls.
compose applies right to left (double then increment gives 11), pipe applies left to right (increment then double gives 12).

js-functions:9.explanation: freeze is shallow: the top-level property can't change (silently ignored in sloppy mode) but nested arrays are still mutable.

js-objects:0.explanation: An instance's [[Prototype]] points to the constructor's prototype property, accessible via __proto__ or Object.getPrototypeOf. A function is itself an object whose prototype is Function.prototype.
Writing creates an own property that shadows the prototype's. Deleting it exposes the inherited one again, so x is still found through the chain but isn't an own property.
The prototype chain ends at Object.prototype, whose own prototype is null.

js-objects:1.explanation: The second argument of Object.create takes property descriptors. enumerable: false hides the property from keys and JSON.stringify, but it's still readable.

js-objects:2.explanation: super() runs the parent constructor, which calls the overridden init via the instance's prototype chain, before the child constructor sets its own n, so n is still 'A' when B.init runs.
Classes are functions. Static methods are inherited because the child constructor's prototype is the parent constructor.

js-objects:2.code:

try { A(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name); }
js-objects:2.explanation: Class constructors can't be called without new, and calling one throws a TypeError. The second call never runs because the first throws in the try block.

js-objects:3.explanation: A leading # makes a field truly private, so c.secret is just an undefined normal property. The setter doubles the value, and static fields are shared on the class.

js-objects:3.code:

console.log(T.has(new T()), T.has({}));
js-objects:3.explanation: The #x in obj brand check tests whether an object has a given private field without throwing.

js-objects:4.explanation: defineProperty defaults all flags to false: the property isn't writable, enumerable or configurable, so the assignment is silently ignored in sloppy mode.
Frozen objects reject writes and deletions, sealed ones allow changing existing values but not adding or removing properties. In strict mode violations throw. A frozen object is also sealed.

js-objects:5.explanation: A JSON round trip turns Dates into strings and drops functions and undefined values. It's not a faithful deep clone. structuredClone keeps Dates but throws on functions.
Spread copies one level, so c.n is the same object as a.n (v becomes 3) while the primitive k is copied. A JSON round trip creates an independent copy, so changing d leaves a alone.

js-objects:6.explanation: Object comparison is by reference. == converts an object to a primitive when the other side is a primitive, so [1] == 1 and the String wrapper == 'a' are true, but === never converts.
Arguments are passed by value, but the value is a reference. Mutating through it affects the caller; reassigning the parameter only rebinds the local name.

js-objects:7.explanation: Map keys keep their type (1 and '1' are different) and use SameValueZero, so NaN equals NaN. Object keys are coerced to strings, so 1 and '1' collide. Set also treats NaN as one value.
Objects as keys are compared by identity. WeakMap holds keys weakly so it can't be iterated and has no size property.

js-async:0.explanation: The callback is scheduled for a later turn of the event loop, so the synchronous log runs first.

js-async:1.code:
Promise.resolve(1)
  .then((v) => { throw new Error('x'); })
  .then(() => console.log('skipped'))
  .catch((e) => e.message)
  .then((v) => console.log('after', v))
  .finally(() => console.log('fin'));
js-async:1.explanation: A throw rejects the chain and skips .then handlers until a catch. The catch returns a value, so the chain recovers and continues with it. finally runs last.

js-async:1.code:
const p = new Promise((res, rej) => { res('a'); rej('b'); res('c'); });
p.then(console.log).catch(console.log);
js-async:1.explanation: A promise settles only once. After the first resolve, later resolve or reject calls are ignored.
A non-function argument to then is ignored, so the value 1 passes through. The two chains each take the same number of microtask ticks, so they log in the order they were created.

js-async:2.explanation: race settles with the first to finish (5 ms), any waits for the first fulfilment (10 ms), and allSettled waits for all of them and never rejects. race logs at 5 ms, then at 10 ms the allSettled timer (created first) fires before the any timer, so the order is fast, statuses, ok.

js-async:2.code:
Promise.all([1, Promise.resolve(2), new Promise((_, r) => setTimeout(() => r('boom'), 0))])
  .then(console.log, (e) => console.log('rejected', e));
js-async:2.explanation: Promise.all rejects as soon as any input rejects, with that reason, and discards the other results.

js-async:3.explanation: The rejection is thrown at the await, so the catch return value is used, but finally runs before the function's promise resolves.
An async function runs synchronously until the first await, then the rest is queued as a microtask, after the current sync code finishes.

js-async:4.explanation: Sync code runs first (1, 5, 7). Then all microtasks in queue order (3, 4, 6), and only after that the timer macrotask (2).
The microtask queue is drained completely, including microtasks queued by microtasks, before the next timer. Timers keep their scheduling order.

js-async:5.explanation: Sync code first, then the nextTick queue, then promise microtasks, and only then timers. nextTick has priority over promise callbacks in Node.

js-advanced:8.prompt: What is a hidden class (shape) in V8, and why does it matter for performance?
options: An internal description of an object's property layout that lets the engine access properties by fixed offsets
A private class declared with #
A class that is hidden from the garbage collector
A cache of compiled bytecode on disk
js-advanced:8.explanation: Objects created with the same properties in the same order share a shape, so property reads can be compiled to a fast offset lookup guarded by an inline cache. Adding properties in different orders creates different shapes and makes access slower (polymorphic or megamorphic).

js-advanced:8.prompt: Which pattern keeps V8 property access monomorphic?
options: Initialise every property in the same order in the constructor
Add properties conditionally after creation
Delete properties when they are no longer needed
Use a different object literal shape per call
js-advanced:8.explanation: Consistent shapes at each access site allow inline caches to stay monomorphic. Deleting properties or varying the order forces dictionary-mode or multiple shapes.

js-advanced:8.prompt: What does the JIT compiler (TurboFan) do?
options: Compiles hot functions to optimised machine code using type feedback gathered by the interpreter
Compiles all code to machine code before it runs
Converts JavaScript to WebAssembly
Removes dead code from your source files on disk
js-advanced:8.explanation: V8 first interprets bytecode (Ignition) and records which types flow through hot code, then optimises with speculation. If an assumption breaks, it deoptimises back to bytecode.

js-advanced:8.prompt: Calling a function with different argument types each time can make it slower because inline caches become polymorphic.
options: True
False
js-advanced:8.explanation: The optimised code is specialised on observed types. Mixed types widen the cache and may cause deoptimisation, which is why performance-sensitive code keeps types stable.
